meta_desc: A-Level Geography adventure on water cycle stores, fluxes and residence times.
final_note: 97 percent of Earth's water is in oceans.

walkthroughs.body_html: Oceans 97 percent; ice 2 percent; groundwater 0.6 percent; surface fresh water (rivers, lakes) 0.3 percent; atmosphere 0.001 percent. Of fresh water only, 69 percent is in ice. Fresh available liquid water (rivers, lakes, accessible groundwater) is just 0.7 percent of all water.

Global evaporation ~500000 km^3/yr; precipitation balances over years. Oceans evaporate 425000 km^3/yr; receive only 385000 km^3/yr from precipitation. The 40000 km^3 difference flows back as runoff from land. Powers global atmospheric circulation.

Atmospheric vapour 9 days; rivers 16 days; soils weeks-months; lakes years; groundwater 100-10000 years; ice sheets 100000 years; oceans 3200 years. Shorter residence means greater sensitivity to disturbance.

mcqs.q: Is the amount of water on Earth decreasing as we use it?
options: No — the global total is essentially fixed and cycles between stores; the issue is where water is, in what form, and how fast it transfers, not the planet running dry.
Carbon emitted at night falls back to the ground by morning.
Most of Earth's water escapes to space each year.
Using water destroys it permanently.

mcqs.q: Does carbon stay in the place where it is emitted?
options: CO2 released by a country stays in the air above that country.
No — carbon moves between the atmosphere, oceans, biosphere and soils through fluxes such as photosynthesis, respiration, ocean uptake and combustion; sinks absorb a large share of human emissions.
Carbon emitted at night falls back to the ground by morning.
Carbon and water never occur in the same places.

mcqs.q: Are the water and carbon cycles independent of each other?
options: No — they interlink: vegetation transpires water while storing carbon, oceans absorb both heat and CO2, and carbon-driven climate change alters precipitation and evaporation.
Most of Earth's water escapes to space each year.
Carbon and water never occur in the same places.
The two cycles can be studied as completely separate systems.
